newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Embarrassed Japan extends minister's stay at WTO.
newsitem.headline: Embarrassed Japan extends minister's stay at WTO.

text.p: Global peer pressure and domestic criticism on Tuesday forced Japan to extend its foreign minister's brief stay at a meeting here of a global organisation long lauded by Tokyo as vital to world free trade.
Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda will extend his stay until late Wednesday evening at the first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), the ministry said in a statement.
He arrived early on Tuesday, the second day of the week-long gathering, and had been due to go home the same evening.

Japan suffered a major embarrassment and a blow to its hopes of playing a high-profile role at the WTO meeting after its trade minister was trapped at home by a domestic scandal linking bureaucrats at his ministry to an oil wholesaler arrested on suspicion of tax evasion.
Ikeda had also pleaded the pressure of parliamentary business for his original plan to stay only a day.

"In order for Japan to play an important role in supporting and strengthening the multilateral trade system and to respond to many requests from other countries for bilateral meetings, we have decided to extend the minster's stay," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.

"Asian countries especially have very high expectations and there was concern he could not meet those expectations if he was here just one day. Also, several countries want to hold bilateral meetings."
Japanese journalists have consistently questioned the impact of Japan's low ministerial profile on its influence at the WTO meeting.

Ikeda began his stay with an appeal to WTO members to forge a deal to scrap tariffs on a host of information technologies as well as include investment and competition issues on the global trade watchdog's future agenda.

"I ardently hope that we will have an agreement (on eliminating tariffs on information technology) as the most significant achievement of this ministerial conference in the area of trade liberalisation," Ikeda said in a speech on Tuesday morning.
In marked contrast to the big crowds which listened to Monday's speeches by U.S., European and other trade ministers, Ikeda's remarks played before a sparse and scattered audience.
Trade negotiators and diplomats have sought to put the best face on their delegation's low political profile, but some admitted privately that they were unhappy.
Still, prospects looked relatively good for Japan to obtain some items on its WTO wish list despite the trade minister's absence and Ikeda's brief appearance.

Ministers from the Big Four trade powers -- the United States, the European Union, Japan and Canada -- were meeting over lunch to try to thrash out a broad deal on an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) which they hope other WTO members, especially Asian-Pacific nations, will then join.
Tokyo strongly backs the U.S.-led infotech initiative, a natural stance given that together the two nations account for over one-third of the world's exports in the lucrative and fast-growing market.
Key WTO countries also appeared to be nearing agreement on including a study of competition policy in the WTO's future agenda.

"No one said that we should not do this," a Japanese Foreign Ministry official told reporters after ministers from about 25 nations met late Tuesday morning to talk about it. "We have come to the point where we are approaching a compromise."
